items.title: CVE-2026-119977 (Tier 2)
items.excerpt: General infrastructure RCE in widely deployed WordPress CMS, explicitly noted as impacting government, healthcare, and finance public-facing sites.

items.title: Unmasking EvilTokens: Getting to the root of device code phishing
items.excerpt: Analyzes the EvilTokens framework, detailing how attackers exploit OAuth device code flows to bypass MFA and steal valid authentication tokens. Provides technical breakdowns of the phishing infrastructure, proxy configurations, and mitigation strategies for identity administrators managing enterprise access controls.

items.title: Breaking the code: Multi-stage ‘code of conduct’ phishing campaign leads to AiTM token compromise
items.excerpt: Details a sophisticated multi-stage campaign leveraging fake compliance portals to deploy Adversary-in-the-Middle proxies. Explains how attackers capture session cookies and tokens in real-time, offering detection rules, conditional access tuning, and architectural defenses for enterprise identity platforms.

items.title: Device Code Phishing is an Evolution in Identity Takeover
items.excerpt: Explores how device code phishing has matured into a primary vector for identity takeover, circumventing traditional MFA controls. Discusses threat actor infrastructure, user interaction patterns, and strategic controls like token lifetime restrictions and OAuth consent monitoring for infrastructure defenders.

items.title: Inside an AI‑enabled device code phishing campaign
items.excerpt: Investigates a campaign leveraging generative AI to craft highly personalized lures that drive victims to device code authentication prompts. Analyzes AI-generated content patterns, infrastructure scaling, and identity-centric detection strategies to neutralize automated phishing operations targeting cloud environments.

items.title: MadApe: The Code That Opens the Door
items.excerpt: Reverse-engineers the MadApe phishing kit, revealing its automated infrastructure for harvesting Microsoft device codes. Covers deployment mechanics, proxy configurations, and actionable telemetry for SOC teams to block kit-hosted domains and monitor for anomalous OAuth consent events across tenant networks.

items.title: The ‘code of conduct’ phishing campaign: What MSPs need to know right now
items.excerpt: Examines the operational tactics behind the widespread compliance-themed phishing wave targeting managed service providers. Highlights infrastructure-level indicators, email filtering bypass techniques, and recommended response playbooks for MSP security teams managing multi-tenant client environments.

items.title: Joint advisory: state-sponsored spear-phishing campaigns targeting critical infrastructure - SUVAT
items.excerpt: Five Eyes joint advisory outlining state-sponsored spearphishing operations targeting critical infrastructure sectors. Covers campaign infrastructure, initial access tactics, and cross-agency recommendations for network segmentation, email security posture, and incident response coordination for high-value assets.

items.title: Foreign Threat Actor Conducting Large-Scale Spearphishing Campaign with RDP Attachments | CISA
items.excerpt: CISA alert on a large-scale campaign distributing malicious RDP files to establish remote access. Details file characteristics, execution chains, and defensive measures including attachment filtering, RDP hardening, and endpoint detection rules for infrastructure teams managing hybrid workloads.

items.title: CVE-2026-115830
items.excerpt: In Secret Server versions earlier than 12.3.1, a user under certain conditions could submit an unsigned JWT and receive cloudadmin permissions in response.

items.title: CVE-2026-115829
items.excerpt: In Secret Server versions earlier than 12.3.1, a user could bypass the initial login step and authenticate by successfully negotiating the second factor login step only.

items.title: CVE-2026-119572
items.excerpt: Traefik from 3.7.0-ea.1 before 3.7.15 contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the Kubernetes Ingress NGINX provider that silently disables mTLS configured via the auth-tls-secret annotation. When another Ingress declares a path on the same host without matching auth-tls settings, Traefik falls back to default TLS options, letting unauthenticated attackers reach backends requiring client certificates.
